about: Simulator: reading and building phylogenetic trees. Three prepared trees to read (two cladograms from body characters, one tree from DNA differences with branch lengths) and three character tables to build from. The student rotates nodes, finds most recent common ancestors and sister groups, tests whether a set of taxa is a clade, places shared derived characters on branches and builds a tree, all with buttons, checkboxes and lists. Model code: bio/assets/tools/bio-tool-math.js (ApBioMath.phylo). Validator: scripts/lib/apbio-tool-checks/tree-reading.mjs checks every tree against its own character table, rotation invariance and branch lengths, and recomputes the stimulus tables and the facts each question keys.
intro: Read a family tree of species. Turn branches around a branch point and see that the relationships stay the same, find the most recent common ancestor of any taxa, test whether a group is a clade, mark where each shared derived character evolved, and build a tree yourself from a table of characters. Every step works with buttons and lists, and every tree has a written description. The questions below use the same trees.
howItWorks:
A phylogenetic tree is a hypothesis about how species are related. Read it from the root (the oldest common ancestor, at the left) toward the tips (the living taxa, at the right).

  • Each node (branch point) stands for a common ancestor that split into two or more lineages. The nodes here are numbered so you can name them; node 1 is the root.
  • The most recent common ancestor of a set of taxa is the node closest to the tips that has all of them among its descendants.
  • A clade (a monophyletic group) is an ancestor and all of its descendants: every tip beyond one node. Two clades that split from the same node are sister groups.
  • A group that is not a clade: the tool calls it paraphyletic when it leaves out one clade of its common ancestor's descendants (like "fish" without the four-limbed animals), and polyphyletic when its members come from separate branches and their common ancestor's other descendants are scattered among them.
  • Rotating a node swaps the order of the branches that come out of it, like spinning a mobile. The tips move up or down the page, but every node keeps the same descendants, so the relationships do not change. Taxa next to each other on the page are not necessarily close relatives.
  • A shared derived character is a trait that appeared in a common ancestor and is inherited by all its descendants (unless lost later). Each one is marked on the branch leading to the clade that has it. A character only one taxon has marks that taxon's own branch and says nothing about grouping. A trait every taxon in the table shares, or one the outgroup also has, does not help either.
  • The outgroup branched off before all the others. It shows which state of each character is the older one: whatever the outgroup has is treated as ancestral.
  • Building a tree from a table: the taxa sharing a derived character form a clade, and a character shared by fewer taxa marks a clade nested inside. The tool accepts your tree if it has exactly the clades the table supports, in any rotation.
  • Branch lengths. In a cladogram (the body-character trees) only the branching order matters; the tips are lined up on the right. In the DNA tree each branch is drawn to scale: its length is the percent of DNA bases that changed along it.
  • A tree is a hypothesis: new data can move a branch. The tool has no randomness, so the same steps always give the same results.

trees.title: Seven chordates (body characters)
trees.about: A cladogram built from body characters. The lancelet, a small filter-feeding animal with a stiff rod (notochord) but no backbone, is the outgroup: it branched off before the others and lacks every derived character in the table.

characters.name: Amnion (a fluid-filled membrane around the embryo)

trees.title: Six plants (body characters)
trees.about: A cladogram built from body characters. A charophyte, a green alga that lives in fresh water, is the outgroup: land plants evolved from algae like it, and it lacks every derived character in the table.

characters.name: Embryo kept and fed inside the parent plant

trees.title: Six primates (DNA differences)
trees.about: A phylogenetic tree built from DNA. Each branch is drawn as long as the number of DNA changes along it, so the distance between two tips, traced along the branches, is the percent of DNA bases that differ between them. The values are rounded teaching values, close to published genome comparisons. The root sits between the apes and the two monkeys.

trees.title: Six invented species, P to U (build only)
trees.about: Invented species with numbered characters, for practice. Species P is the outgroup and lacks every derived character.

tr-s1.title: A plant character table and primate DNA
tr-s1.text:
Table 1 lists four characters in six plants (Yes = the plant has it). The charophyte alga, a freshwater green alga, is the outgroup. Table 2 gives the percent of DNA bases that differ between five primates; these are rounded teaching values, close to published genome comparisons.

A student drew the tree supported by Table 1 twice. In Drawing 1 the tips read from top to bottom: charophyte alga, moss, fern, pine, rose, grass. In Drawing 2 the student rotated two nodes, the one where rose and grass split and the one where pine splits from them, so the tips read: charophyte alga, moss, fern, grass, rose, pine.

tables.caption: Table 1. Characters of six plants
cols: Embryo kept and fed inside the parent plant

tables.caption: Table 2. Percent of DNA bases that differ between five primates

questions.q: Which statement about the plants in Table 1 is best supported by their shared derived characters?
options: Rose and grass share a more recent common ancestor with each other than either shares with pine
Moss and the charophyte alga form a clade, because both lack vascular tissue
Pine is the ancestor of rose and grass, because it has seeds but no flowers
Fern is more closely related to moss than to pine, because fern and moss both lack seeds

why.correct: Rose and grass share every derived character pine has (embryo, vascular tissue, seeds) plus one more, flowers and fruit. The ancestor in which flowers appeared is shared only by rose and grass, so it is more recent than the ancestor all three seed plants share.
options: Right: a derived character only rose and grass share marks their own, more recent common ancestor.

Lacking vascular tissue is the ancestral state, shared with the outgroup; a shared ancestral trait does not mark a clade, and moss shares the derived embryo character with the other land plants, not with the alga.
Every taxon in the table is a living tip; a tip is never the ancestor of another tip. Pine and the flowering plants share a common ancestor that had seeds.
Lacking seeds is ancestral; fern shares the derived vascular tissue with pine, rose and grass, so it is closer to them than to moss.

questions.q: A student groups moss and fern together as "seedless plants." Which statement about this group is correct?
options: It is not a clade, because the most recent common ancestor of moss and fern is also the ancestor of pine, rose and grass, which the group leaves out
It is a clade, because both moss and fern lack seeds
It is a clade, because moss and fern are drawn next to each other on the tree
It is not a clade, because moss lacks vascular tissue and fern has it

why.correct: A clade is an ancestor and all its descendants. The most recent common ancestor of moss and fern is the first land plant on the tree, and its descendants also include pine, rose and grass. Leaving out the seed plants makes "seedless plants" a paraphyletic group, defined by a missing trait rather than a shared derived one.
options: Right: the group leaves out some descendants of its common ancestor, so it is not a clade.
Lacking seeds is the ancestral state, which the alga outgroup shares too; a shared ancestral trait does not define a clade.
Position on the page changes when nodes are rotated; closeness is read from shared ancestors, not from neighboring tips.
Members of a clade can differ in many traits; what matters is whether the group includes every descendant of its common ancestor, and this one does not.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares Drawing 1 and Drawing 2 of the plant tree?
options: Both drawings show the same relationships, because rotating a node changes the order of the tips but not which taxa share each common ancestor
In Drawing 2 fern is more closely related to grass than to pine, because fern and grass are now next to each other
In Drawing 2 pine is the most recently evolved plant, because it is now at the bottom of the tree
Drawing 2 is a different hypothesis, because pine now branches off after rose and grass

why.correct: Rotating a node only swaps the branches that come out of it. Every node still has the same descendants: rose and grass still share the most recent ancestor, pine still joins them at the next node down, and fern still joins the seed plants below that. The order of tips on the page carries no information.
options: Right: rotation changes the drawing, not the tree.
Fern joins the seed plants at the same node in both drawings, so it is equally related to grass and pine; being next to grass on the page does not change that.
All the tips are living taxa; their order on the page does not show which evolved most recently.
Pine still splits from the rose and grass clade at the same node; only the order of the tips changed.

questions.q: Which tree is best supported by the DNA differences in Table 2?
options: Human and chimpanzee are sister groups, gorilla is the sister group of that pair, orangutan joins next, and the macaque is outside the apes
Human and gorilla are sister groups, with chimpanzee joining next, because humans and gorillas are both large ground-living apes
Chimpanzee and gorilla are sister groups, and human branches off before them
Human, chimpanzee, gorilla and orangutan all split from one ancestor at the same time, with the macaque outside

why.correct: The fewer DNA differences two taxa have, the more recently they shared an ancestor. Human and chimpanzee differ least (1.2%), so they are sister groups; gorilla differs from both by the same 1.6%, so it joins that pair next; orangutan differs from all three by 3.1%; the macaque differs from all four apes by 6.4%.
options: Right: the smallest differences pair the most recent relatives, step by step.
Human and gorilla differ by 1.6%, more than human and chimpanzee (1.2%); body size and habitat are not the data in the table.
Chimpanzee and gorilla differ by 1.6%, more than chimpanzee and human (1.2%), so chimpanzee pairs with human first.
The apes differ from each other by different amounts (1.2%, 1.6%, 3.1%), which shows the lineages split at different times, not all at once.

questions.q: Assume DNA differences build up at a constant rate (a molecular clock) and that the human and chimpanzee lineages split about 6 million years ago. Using Table 2, estimate how many million years ago the orangutan lineage split from the lineage leading to humans. Round to one decimal place.

why.correct: With a constant rate, time since a split is proportional to the DNA difference. Human and orangutan differ by 3.1%, and human and chimpanzee by 1.2%, so the orangutan split is 3.1 / 1.2 = 2.58 times older: 2.58 × 6 = 15.5 million years ago. Real estimates vary with the data and the calibration used.

frq.title: Mini free-response question: building a plant tree

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the outgroup in Table 1 and describe how it is used to decide which state of each character is derived.

rubric.point: Identifies the charophyte alga as the outgroup and describes that a character state it has is treated as ancestral, so the other state (present, here) is derived.
accept: the alga lacks all four characters, so having them is derived
the alga branched off first and shows the older states

parts.sample: The charophyte alga is the outgroup. It branched off before the land plants, so the state it has for each character is treated as the ancestral one. It lacks all four characters, so having each character is the derived state.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain, using shared derived characters, why rose and grass are placed as each other's closest relatives, with pine as their sister group.

rubric.point: Explains that rose and grass share a derived character no other taxon has (flowers and fruit), which marks their most recent common ancestor.
accept: only rose and grass have flowers
flowers evolved in the ancestor of rose and grass

rubric.point: Explains that pine shares seeds (and vascular tissue and the embryo) with rose and grass but not flowers, so it joins them at an older node, as their sister group.
accept: seeds group pine with rose and grass
pine lacks flowers, so it branched off before flowers evolved

parts.sample: Rose and grass are the only plants with flowers and fruit, a derived character, so flowers must have appeared in an ancestor they share with no other plant in the table: they are each other's closest relatives. Pine has seeds, vascular tissue and a protected embryo, the derived characters rose and grass also have, but not flowers. So pine shares an older common ancestor with them, the one in which seeds appeared, and pine is the sister group of the rose and grass clade.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A newly described plant has an embryo kept in the parent and vascular tissue, but no seeds and no flowers. Predict where it joins the tree supported by Table 1, and justify your prediction.

rubric.point: Predicts it joins inside the vascular-plant clade (with fern, pine, rose and grass) but outside the seed-plant clade, and justifies it with the shared derived characters (has vascular tissue, lacks seeds); accepts that its exact relationship to fern is not resolved by these characters.
accept: next to fern, below the seed plants
with fern, outside pine, rose and grass

parts.sample: It joins the clade of vascular plants, branching off below the seed plants, near the fern. It shares the derived embryo and vascular tissue characters with fern, pine, rose and grass, so it belongs to that clade, but it lacks seeds, so it is outside the clade of pine, rose and grass. These four characters cannot tell whether it is closer to fern or to the seed plants, so it and fern would join the same node.
